text: Everything we know comes from [[fossil|fossils]], traces of life saved in rock.
Fossils aren't only bones. Footprints, eggs, nests, skin prints and even poo all tell stories.

Scientists work like detectives, putting many small clues together into one picture. The evidence now includes many thousands of fossils, from every continent on Earth, found and checked by scientists in many countries.

spots: The most famous clue. Bones show size, shape and how an animal moved.
Trackways show how dinosaurs walked, how fast, and sometimes that they travelled in groups.
Eggs tell us dinosaurs laid eggs, and how they arranged their nests.
Called coprolite. It shows what dinosaurs ate.
Some fossils keep the pattern of scales, like a stamp in mud.
Tooth marks on bones show who tried to eat whom.

d.try: Ask a friend to hide a few objects in a tray of sand, such as a spoon, a toy car and a shell. Without looking, uncover them slowly with a paintbrush. Try to guess each object from the first small bit you see. That's how fossil hunters work, from part of a bone to the whole animal.
myth: Dinosaurs are mostly made up from one or two bones.
Some dinosaurs are known from only a few bones, and scientists say so. But others, like T. rex, Triceratops and Maiasaura, are known from dozens or even hundreds of skeletons, some nearly complete.

sec.t:
People found dinosaur bones long before anyone knew what they were. In China, big fossil bones were called [[@myths-chinese|dragon bones]]. In 1677, an English museum keeper named Robert Plot drew part of a huge thigh bone and guessed it came from a giant human. Today we know it was from Megalosaurus.

Some historians think that [[@myths-giants|ancient legends of griffins]] in Central Asia may have been inspired by skulls of beaked dinosaurs eroding out of the desert. It is an interesting idea, though hard to prove.

In the early 1800s, scientists began comparing fossil bones with the bones of living animals. The French scientist Georges Cuvier showed that some fossils came from animals that no longer existed anywhere. In 1824, William Buckland named Megalosaurus. A year later, the English doctor Gideon Mantell named Iguanodon, from teeth found in Sussex, some of them reportedly spotted by his wife, Mary Ann. They looked like an iguana's teeth, only many times bigger. In 1842, Richard Owen grouped these strange [[reptile|reptiles]] together and called them dinosaurs.

Since then, over 1,000 kinds of dinosaur have been named. Some are known from a single tooth. Others, like T. rex, are known from dozens of skeletons. Each new find can confirm or overturn earlier ideas, which is how science should work.

Footprints show how animals moved. Long gaps between prints mean running. Many parallel tracks mean a herd walking together. In 1976, a zoologist worked out a way to estimate speed from the spacing of [[@dino-feet-tracks|footprints]] and the size of the feet.

India alone has almost every kind of clue. There are bones from Jabalpur, found in 1828, nests of eggs in Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat, footprints in Rajasthan and fossil poo from Maharashtra. Each was found by different people, at different times, yet they fit together.

Other clues show behaviour. Tooth marks on bones show who tried to eat whom. Eggs and nests show how dinosaurs raised their young. [[@dino-poop|Fossil poo]] shows what they had for lunch.

Scientists also study the rock around the fossil to learn whether it was a river, a desert or a lake. See [[@ancient-env|how rocks are diaries]]. Layers of volcanic ash above and below a fossil can be dated, so scientists know [[@fossil-age|how old it is]].

It is the same way [[@history-sources|historians]] and [[@archaeology|archaeologists]] work with the human past. No single clue proves everything. But when bones, tracks, eggs, rocks and dates all agree, the picture becomes very hard to doubt.

सदियों तक लोग कहानियों से, या इससे कि समुद्र को खारा होने में कितना समय लगा होगा, धरती की उम्र का अंदाज़ा लगाते रहे। उनके आँकड़े बहुत ही छोटे थे। 1650 में आयरलैंड के एक आर्चबिशप जेम्स अशर ने बाइबिल में दी पीढ़ियों को जोड़कर ईसा पूर्व 4004 का साल निकाला। 1860 के दशक में ब्रिटिश भौतिकविद लॉर्ड केल्विन ने हिसाब लगाया कि लाल-गर्म धरती को ठंडा होने में कितना समय लगेगा, और जवाब आया कुछ करोड़ साल। उन्हें धरती के बहुत अंदर [[radioactive|रेडियोधर्मी]] परमाणुओं से बनने वाली गर्मी के बारे में पता नहीं था।

प्राचीन हिंदू ग्रंथ समय को बिल्कुल अलग ढंग से बताते हैं, विशाल, बार-बार दोहराए जाने वाले चक्रों में। ब्रह्मा का एक दिन, जिसे कल्प कहते हैं, 432 करोड़ साल का होता है। यह धार्मिक विचार है, नाप नहीं, पर इसका पैमाना असली उम्र के काफ़ी करीब है।

20वीं सदी में वैज्ञानिकों को पता चला कि कुछ [[atom|परमाणु]] एक तय रफ़्तार से बदलते हैं। चट्टानों और उल्कापिंडों में उन्हें नापकर धरती की असली उम्र निकली। 1913 में ब्रिटिश भूवैज्ञानिक आर्थर होम्स ने चट्टानों के यूरेनियम से दिखाया कि धरती 100 करोड़ साल से भी कहीं ज़्यादा पुरानी होगी, केल्विन के अंदाज़े से बहुत ज़्यादा। शुरू में बहुत-से वैज्ञानिकों को यह बात हज़म नहीं हुई।

सबसे अहम नाप अमेरिकी वैज्ञानिक क्लेयर पैटरसन ने 1956 में ली। उन्होंने एरिज़ोना के कैन्यन डियाब्लो से मिले एक उल्कापिंड में सीसे की जाँच की और लगभग 455 करोड़ साल का आँकड़ा पाया, जो आज के आँकड़े के बहुत करीब है। इसी दौरान उन्हें पता चला कि गाड़ियों के पेट्रोल के सीसे ने लगभग हर चीज़ को [[contaminate|दूषित]] कर दिया है, उनकी प्रयोगशाला की धूल तक को। उन्होंने सालों तक सीसे वाले पेट्रोल के ख़िलाफ़ मुहिम चलाई। बाद में बहुत-से देशों में इस पर रोक लगी, और इससे [[@air-pollution|वायु प्रदूषण]] घटाने में मदद मिली।

धरती का इतिहास इतना लंबा है कि डायनासोरों ने 16.5 करोड़ साल राज किया, फिर भी यह उसका 4% से भी कम है। [[@dino-age-span|डायनासोरों के दौर को पास से देखो]]।

अब सब कुछ एक दिन में समेट दो, आधी रात से शुरू करके। सीधा-सादा जीवन भोर से पहले समुद्रों में आ जाता है। खोल और आँखों वाले जानवर रात लगभग नौ बजे तक नहीं दिखते। डायनासोर पौने ग्यारह के आसपास आते हैं और 23:39 पर ग़ायब हो जाते हैं। आज के इंसान, जो लगभग 3 लाख साल पहले आए, आधी रात से बस छह सेकंड पहले दिखते हैं। हर राजा, हर युद्ध, हर आविष्कार, जिसके बारे में तुमने पढ़ा है, एक सेकंड के आख़िरी छोटे-से टुकड़े में हुआ।

भूवैज्ञानिक इस विशाल फैलाव को "गहरा समय" कहते हैं। इसमें सोचना सीखना विज्ञान के बड़े विचारों में से एक है, ठीक वैसे ही जैसे यह समझना कि धरती सूरज के चारों ओर घूमती है।

text: Gaganyaan, meaning "sky vehicle" in [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]], is India's human spaceflight programme. Its aim is to launch two or three astronauts on an Indian rocket, from [[@isro-launch|Sriharikota]] in Andhra Pradesh, into [[orbit|orbit]] about 400 km above Earth. They would circle the planet for up to three days, then return in a capsule that splashes down in the sea.

If it succeeds, India will become the fourth country to send people into space on its own, after the Soviet Union in 1961, the United States in 1961 and China in 2003. [[@isro-missions|ISRO]] is testing each part carefully first: the rocket, the capsule, the [[@parachutes|parachutes]] and an escape system to save the crew if something goes wrong.

sec.t:
In February 2024, India named the four astronaut-designates for Gaganyaan. All four are test pilots from the Indian Air Force: Prasanth Balakrishnan Nair, Ajit Krishnan, Angad Pratap and Shubhanshu Shukla. They [[@astronaut-training|trained in Russia and in Bengaluru]], learning everything from spacecraft systems to how to survive if the capsule lands somewhere unexpected.

In June 2025, Shukla flew to the [[@space-station|International Space Station]] on a private mission called Axiom-4, launched from the United States. He became the first Indian to visit the station, and the experience he brought home is feeding into Gaganyaan.

The most important part of any crewed rocket is the part you hope never to use: the crew escape system. If the rocket fails, small powerful motors pull the capsule away and parachutes bring it down.

On 21 October 2023, ISRO tested this with a special test rocket from Sriharikota. At about 12 km up, the escape system fired, pulled away a test capsule, and brought it down under parachutes into the Bay of Bengal, where the Navy recovered it. ISRO has also dropped capsules from helicopters to test the parachutes.

The [[@rockets-how|rocket]] chosen to carry the crew is a strengthened version of LVM3, India's heaviest launcher, the same type that sent [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-3]] to the Moon.

[[@indian-astronauts|India's first astronaut]], Rakesh Sharma, flew to the Soviet Salyut 7 space station in April 1984, on a Soviet Soyuz rocket. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi spoke to him by video link and asked [[@earth-from-space|how India looked from space]]. He replied, "Saare jahan se achha", better than the whole world, a line from a famous patriotic song. He spent nearly eight days in orbit and did yoga exercises to study how the body copes without weight.

India's space programme was started in the 1960s by [[@vikram-sarabhai|Vikram Sarabhai]], who believed space technology should help ordinary people through weather forecasts, communication and education. Human spaceflight was a later dream.

ISRO has said it aims to fly the first Gaganyaan crew in 2027. By November 2026, though, the first uncrewed test flight, with Vyommitra on board, had not yet launched. India's longer-term plans include its own space station, the Bharatiya Antariksh Station, by 2035, and an Indian astronaut on the Moon by 2040.

text: Fast. A honeybee beats its wings about 230 times a second, a housefly about 200, and some mosquitoes 600 to 800 times. That is why insects buzz and whine. The sound you hear is the air being pushed by wings moving too quickly to see. Faster wings make a higher note, as you can read in [[@sound-travel|how sound travels]].

Not all insects are so fast. Big butterflies may flap fewer than 20 times a second, and you can watch each beat. In general, the smaller the wing, the faster it needs to move. A tiny wing has less surface to push the air with, so it must make up for it with speed.

d.try: Listen for wing music. On a warm evening, sit near a flowering plant or open window and listen to different insects fly past. A low hum usually means big, slow wings, such as a bumblebee. A thin whine means tiny, fast wings, such as a mosquito.
myth: Scientists once proved that bumblebees shouldn't be able to fly.

The story comes from a rough calculation in the 1930s that treated a bee's wing like a stiff aeroplane wing. Real insect wings flap, twist and make swirls of air that give extra lift. Bees fly perfectly well, and scientists now understand how.

sec.t:
An insect wing does not just flap up and down. It sweeps forwards and backwards and flips over at each end of the stroke, a bit like a swimmer's hand. As it sweeps, it creates a small whirl of air along its front edge. That whirl lowers the pressure above the wing and gives extra lift.

In 2017, scientists filmed mosquitoes with very fast cameras. They found mosquito wings move through only a small arc, but rotate cleverly at each end. The rotation creates extra swirls that help keep the insect up. Honeybees use their wings for more than flying: they also fan them to cool the hive, and they [[@bees-dance|dance]] to share directions.

Houseflies and mosquitoes have only two wings. Their back pair has shrunk into two tiny knobs on stalks, called halteres. As the fly moves, the halteres buzz up and down very fast. When the fly turns, they get twisted slightly, and sense organs at their base notice. This tells the fly at once that it is spinning, a bit like a built-in gyroscope.

Halteres help explain why flies are so hard to swat. A fly also sees fast movement very well. Studies with [[@how-cameras-speed|high-speed cameras]] showed that a fly can spot a threat and plan its escape in a fraction of a second. It shifts its legs so that it leaps away from the danger as it takes off.

Insects were the first animals to fly, more than 300 million years ago. That was long before pterosaurs, birds or bats. Some ancient griffinflies, relatives of dragonflies, had wings about 70 cm across, wider than two school rulers laid end to end.

Some insects fly very far. Globe skimmer dragonflies cross the Indian Ocean between India and East Africa, a trip that takes several generations to complete. In North America, [[@monarch-migration|monarch butterflies]] fly thousands of kilometres to Mexico, and you can read about their lives in [[@butterflies-life|the butterfly's life cycle]].

text: Ball lightning is a rare glowing sphere that sometimes appears during thunderstorms. People describe it as about the size of a grapefruit or a football, glowing white, yellow, orange or blue. It floats or drifts sideways, often for a few seconds, and then fades away or vanishes with a pop.

For centuries, scientists weren't sure it was real, because nobody could predict where it would show up. Then in 2012, researchers in China recorded one by chance. It proved that the glowing balls exist. What makes them is still argued over.

sec.t:
Reports go back hundreds of years. In 1638, during a great thunderstorm in the village of Widecombe-in-the-Moor in England, people described a huge ball of fire crashing into the church during a service.

Modern accounts are calmer. People have seen glowing balls float through open windows, roll along fences or bounce off the ground. Pilots have described balls appearing inside aircraft cabins and drifting down the aisle. Most witnesses say it moved slowly and made little heat.

In a 1960s survey of about 2,000 NASA workers, roughly one in twenty said they had seen it. Since it is so brief, almost nobody has a camera ready.

That matched an idea from two New Zealand scientists, John Abrahamson and James Dinniss. In 2000 they suggested that when lightning hits the ground, it can boil a little soil into a cloud of tiny silicon particles.

As those particles meet oxygen in the air, they slowly burn, giving off light. They stick together in a loose fluffy ball, which glows until the fuel runs out. In 2007, researchers in Brazil zapped thin wafers of silicon with electricity and made glowing balls that lasted several seconds.

The soil theory doesn't explain everything. It's hard to see how burning soil could appear inside a closed aeroplane. So scientists have other ideas.

One suggests ball lightning is a bubble of microwave energy trapped inside a shell of [[plasma|plasma]], the glowing electrified gas that makes up lightning. Another, from physicists in Austria in 2010, proposed that some sightings aren't outside the eye at all. Strong magnetic fields from repeated lightning strikes might make the brain see a glowing spot. Doctors can produce flashes of light in people's vision with magnets, so it is possible, explained more in how your [[@brain-works|brain builds what you see]].

sec.h: Why it's so hard to study
sec.t:
Ball lightning can't be ordered on demand. It appears in storms, which are dangerous places to stand with instruments, and it lasts only seconds. Scientists rely on lucky recordings and careful lab experiments.

They also need to rule out other things. Some reports are probably sparks from power lines, St Elmo's fire glowing on ship masts, or the afterimage left in your eyes by a bright flash.

Treat any storm with respect. Government records show that lightning kills more people in India than any other natural hazard, mostly people caught outdoors in the [[monsoon|monsoon]]. If you hear thunder, head indoors and stay away from tall trees, open fields and water.

Buildings with [[@lightning-rods|lightning rods]] are much safer, because the rod gives the electricity an easy path to the ground. Meanwhile the mystery keeps its fans. Over a century ago, the inventor [[@nikola-tesla|Nikola Tesla]] even claimed he had made glowing fireballs in his own lab.

text: When rain falls, some of it runs into rivers and some evaporates. The rest soaks down into the soil. It trickles through sand, gravel and cracks in rock until it reaches a layer where every gap is already full of water. The top of that wet layer is called the water table. A layer of rock or sand that holds plenty of water is an [[aquifer|aquifer]].

A well is a hole that reaches below the water table. Water seeps sideways out of the wet ground and collects at the bottom of the hole. Then you lift it with a bucket, a hand pump or an electric pump. A borewell is the same idea, drilled much narrower and much deeper.

st.reveal: A suction pump works because air pressure pushes water up the pipe. Even a perfect vacuum can only hold up about 10 metres of water, and real pumps manage less. Deep borewells need a pump that sits down in the water and pushes it up.

sec.t:
For most of history, wells were dug by hand. Workers used spades and baskets to make a round shaft a metre or more wide. They lined the walls with stone or brick so the sides wouldn't fall in. A rope, a bucket and a wooden [[pulley|pulley]] did the rest.

For farms, one bucket was never enough. In north India and Pakistan, farmers used the Persian wheel, or *rahat*: a chain of clay or metal pots looped over a wheel. A pair of bullocks or a camel walked in circles to turn it, and the pots came up full and tipped their water into a channel.

India has dug wells for thousands of years. In [[@indus-cities|Mohenjo-daro]], one of the great Indus cities, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] found hundreds of wells lined with wedge-shaped bricks. Many homes seem to have had their own. In dry parts of western India, people later built grand [[@stepwells|stepwells]], with flights of stairs leading down to the water as it rose and fell through the year.

{{story:monsoon}}

A borewell is drilled by a truck-mounted rig. A spinning drill bit, often with hard tips, grinds through soil and rock, while air or water flushes the broken bits up to the surface. The hole may be only 15 centimetres wide. It can go down 100, 200 or even 400 metres in places where the water table has dropped.

Workers fit a pipe called a casing into the top of the hole to stop soil falling in. Then they lower a submersible pump, a long thin electric pump that sits underwater at the bottom. It pushes water up instead of sucking it. That matters, because suction alone can only lift water about 7 or 8 metres.

Across Indian villages you can still see sturdy iron hand pumps. The India Mark II design, developed in the 1970s with help from UNICEF, has its pumping cylinder down inside the well rather than at the top. Each push on the handle lifts a column of water, so it can work from much deeper than an old suction pump.

India pumps more [[@groundwater|groundwater]] than any other country. Most of it waters farms, and many cities depend on it too. In parts of Punjab, Rajasthan and Bengaluru, wells that once struck water at 10 metres now go down hundreds of metres. When people pump out more than rain puts back, the water table falls year after year.

The fix is to help rain soak back in. Every [[@monsoon|monsoon]], water caught in ponds, check dams and pits can seep down and refill the aquifers. [[@rainwater-harvesting|Rainwater harvesting]] from roofs and recharge wells does the same thing in cities.

Old borewells that are left uncovered are dangerous, because their openings are small and easy to miss. India's Supreme Court has ordered that unused borewells must be capped or filled. If you ever see an open hole in a field, keep away and tell an adult straight away.

sec.t:
मोने का जन्म 1840 में [[@paris|पेरिस]] में हुआ, पर वे बड़े हुए ली आव्र में, जो नॉर्मंडी के तट पर एक बंदरगाह है। किशोर उम्र में वे आसपास के लोगों के मज़ेदार कार्टून (कैरिकेचर) बनाकर बेचते थे। प्राकृतिक दृश्य बनाने वाले एक चित्रकार, यूजीन बूदाँ, ने उनका काम देखा और उन्हें खुली हवा में, बाहर जाकर पेंट करने को कहा।

बाहर पेंट करना उन्हीं दिनों आसान हुआ था, [[@art-materials|रंगों और औज़ारों]] में आए एक बदलाव की वजह से। 1841 में अमेरिकी चित्रकार जॉन गॉफ़ रैंड ने धातु की वह ट्यूब बनाई जिसे दबाकर रंग निकाला जा सकता था, जैसे आज टूथपेस्ट निकालते हैं। इससे पहले कलाकार स्टूडियो में ही अपने [[pigment|रंग]] पीसते-घोलते थे और उन्हें सुअर के मूत्राशय से बनी थैलियों में रखते थे, जो रिसती थीं और सूख जाती थीं। ट्यूबों की बदौलत मोने अपने रंग समुद्र तट, खेतों और नदी किनारों तक ले जा सके।

रोशनी कैसे बदलती है, इसकी मोने को धुन सवार थी। 1890 के दशक की शुरुआत में उन्होंने अपने घर के पास एक खेत में भूसे के ढेरों को बार-बार पेंट किया: सुबह की धुंध में, दोपहर में, सूरज ढलते और बर्फ़ के नीचे। फिर रूआँ के बड़े गिरजाघर (कैथेड्रल) का सामने वाला हिस्सा अलग-अलग पहरों में 30 से ज़्यादा बार बनाया।

कभी-कभी वे कई कैनवस पर एक साथ काम करते थे और सूरज खिसकने के साथ कैनवस बदलते जाते थे। वे रंगों को आपस में घोलते नहीं थे, बल्कि उन्हें अगल-बगल लगा देते थे। दूर से देखने पर तुम्हारी आँखें खुद उन्हें मिला लेती हैं। उनकी तस्वीरों में परछाईं धूसर नहीं, नीली या बैंगनी हो सकती थी, क्योंकि उन्हें वैसी ही दिखती थी। यह बात रोशनी और पेंट में [[@colour-mix|रंगों के मिलने]] के तरीके से मेल खाती है।

1883 में मोने पेरिस के पश्चिम में बसे गाँव जिवर्नी आ गए। उन्होंने फूलों का एक बड़ा बगीचा बनाया और बाद में एक तालाब खुदवाया। उसमें कुमुदिनियाँ लगाईं और ऊपर जापानी ढंग का एक पुल बनवाया। उन्हें जापान के लकड़ी के ठप्पों से छपे चित्र बहुत पसंद थे और उन्होंने ऐसे ढेरों चित्र जमा किए। वे आज भी उनके घर में टँगे हैं। उनके सपाट रंगों और ऊपर से या बगल से देखे गए अनोखे नज़ारों ने मोने के अपनी तस्वीरों को सजाने के ढंग पर गहरा असर डाला।

ज़िंदगी के आखिरी 30 सालों में यही तालाब उनका सबसे पसंदीदा [[motif|विषय]] रहा। उन्होंने कुमुदिनियों की लगभग 250 पेंटिंग बनाईं, जिनमें से कुछ बहुत विशाल हैं। ऐसे आठ बड़े-बड़े पैनल आज पेरिस के म्यूज़े दे ल'ओरांजरी के दो अंडाकार कमरों की दीवारों पर घूमते हुए लगे हैं।

सत्तर की उम्र पार करने पर मोने को मोतियाबिंद हो गया। इसमें आँख के अंदर का [[lens|लेंस]] धुँधला पड़ने लगता है। उन्हें रंग मटमैले और पीले-से दिखने लगे, और उनकी पेंटिंग ज़्यादा लाल और खुरदुरी होती गईं। 1923 में उनका ऑपरेशन हुआ। यह उन ऑपरेशनों का शुरुआती रूप था जो आज कुछ ही मिनटों में [[@eyesight-glasses|नज़र]] ठीक कर देते हैं।

1926 में 86 साल की उम्र में जिवर्नी में उनका निधन हुआ। उनका घर और बगीचा अब लोगों के देखने के लिए खुला है। [[@van-gogh|वान गॉग]] जैसे चित्रकारों ने इंप्रेशनिज़्म से बहुत कुछ सीखा। और 2019 में मोने की भूसे के ढेर वाली एक पेंटिंग नीलामी में लगभग 11 करोड़ अमेरिकी डॉलर में बिकी।

text: The G20, or Group of Twenty, is a club of the world's biggest [[economy|economies]]. Its members are 19 countries, including India, the USA, China, Brazil, Japan and Saudi Arabia, plus the European Union and, since 2023, the African Union. Together they make up about 85% of the world economy and about two-thirds of its people.

Their leaders meet once a year at a summit to discuss problems no country can fix alone, such as financial crises, trade, [[climate|climate]] change, debt and health. The G20 can't pass laws. It works by getting powerful countries to agree on shared goals and then nudging each other to follow through.

sec.t:
The 19 member countries are Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, South Korea, Turkey, the UK and the USA. The G20 has no office building and no permanent staff. Instead, the presidency rotates every year. The host country plans hundreds of meetings, sets the themes and holds the leaders' summit at the end.

Each leader has a personal representative called a sherpa, named after [[@people-sherpas|the Sherpa mountain guides]] of Nepal who help climbers reach the top. The sherpas do the hard work of negotiating, line by line, the joint statement leaders sign at the summit. The past, present and next hosts work together as a team of three called the troika, so plans carry over.

India held the presidency from December 2022 to November 2023. Its theme was *Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam*, a Sanskrit phrase meaning "the world is one family", with the motto "One Earth, One Family, One Future".

Instead of holding everything in [[@delhi|Delhi]], India spread more than 200 meetings across about 60 cities, from [[@kashmir|Srinagar]] to Kumarakom. The leaders' summit was held at the new Bharat Mandapam convention centre in Delhi in September 2023. There, leaders agreed a joint declaration and welcomed the African Union as a permanent member.

sec.h: Why it matters, and its critics
sec.t:
When the G20's biggest economies act together, the effect can be large. In 2008 and 2009, their joint spending and rescue plans helped stop the crisis from getting even worse. During the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]], they let the poorest countries pause some debt payments.

Critics say a group of 20 can't speak for nearly 200 countries, and that its promises are often vague and not kept. Others point out that agreeing on anything among rivals like the USA, China and Russia is an achievement in itself. In 2025, South Africa hosted the first G20 summit held in Africa, and in 2026 the presidency passed to the USA. Debates over [[@climate-change|climate change]] and world [[@trade-world|trade]] are likely to fill its agenda for years.

text: Human rights are the basic freedoms and protections every person should have, simply because they are human. They include the right to life and to be free from slavery and torture. They also include the right to speak your mind, follow a religion or none, go to school and be treated fairly by the law.

The most famous list is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, agreed by the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] in 1948. It has 30 articles. The first says, "All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights."
The declaration itself is not a law. But it has shaped [[treaty|treaties]], courts and [[constitution|constitutions]] around the world, including [[@constitution|India's Constitution]].

st.reveal: Hansa Mehta, a campaigner for women's rights and education, sat on the UN commission that wrote the declaration. She argued that "all men" could be read as leaving women out, and the words were changed.

Human rights belong to every person simply for being human. Laws may limit some freedoms in fair, set ways, such as sending someone to prison after a trial, but nobody loses their basic rights, like not being tortured.

sec.t:
The [[@world-war-two|Second World War]] ended in 1945. Tens of millions of people had died, and the [[@holocaust|Holocaust]] had shown how a government could turn on its own people. Many leaders felt the world needed a shared promise that this must never happen again.

The new United Nations set up a commission to write that promise. It was chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, widow of the American president Franklin D. Roosevelt. Members came from China, Lebanon, France, India, Chile and many other countries.

Some rights protect you from being harmed or silenced: [[@free-speech|freedom of speech]], a fair trial and the right to vote. Others are about meeting needs, such as education, health care, food and a safe home.

Countries usually find the first kind easier to promise. The second kind costs money, and poorer countries may struggle to provide it. Both are in the declaration.

Ideas in the declaration grew into later treaties, such as the [[@rights-kids|children's rights]] convention of 1989. Courts in many countries use them in their judgments.

People have often had to struggle for rights that were already written down. The American [[@civil-rights|civil rights]] movement of the 1950s and 1960s fought for equal treatment that the [[@us-constitution|US Constitution]] already seemed to promise.

The UN has a Human Rights Council, where countries review each other's records every few years. Independent experts write reports on problems such as [[@child-labour|child labour]] or the treatment of prisoners.

Many countries also have their own watchdogs. India set up the National Human Rights Commission in 1993. Anyone can complain to it, and it can investigate and recommend action, though it cannot punish people itself. Groups such as Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, which are not run by any government, publish reports too. Governments often dislike these reports, which is partly why they matter.

Every right comes with a responsibility: respecting the same right in others. Your freedom of speech sits beside someone else's right not to be threatened. India's Constitution lists fundamental duties alongside its rights for this reason. Human Rights Day falls on 10 December each year, the day the declaration was adopted.

text: Wherever children have a bit of open ground, they invent games. Some need nothing at all: just running, chasing and hiding. Others need a chalk drawing, a few stones or a stick.

Many games turn up across the world with different names. Tag is pakdam pakdai in Hindi. Hopscotch is stapu or kith-kith in India, rayuela in Latin America and marelle in France. Hide-and-seek is chhupan chhupai. Five stones is gutte in north India and jacks in the US.
Some games belong to one place, like [[@kho-kho|kho-kho]] in India or Red Rover in the US and UK. Kids learn most of them from other kids, not from adults or books.

myth: Hopscotch was invented by Roman soldiers as training for battle.
This story is often repeated, but there is no good evidence for it. Hopping games are old and found in many places, and nobody knows exactly where hopscotch began.

sec.t:
In 1560, the Flemish artist Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted a town square crowded with children. Look closely and you can find about 80 different games. Children play leapfrog, spin tops, walk on stilts, roll hoops, play blind man's buff and ride on each other's shoulders.

The painting hangs in a museum in Vienna. It is one of the most detailed records of children's play from that time, and a favourite puzzle among [[@famous-paintings|famous paintings]]. Many of its games are still played today, nearly 500 years later.

Some games are very old. In [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greece]], children played knucklebones, tossing and catching the small ankle bones of sheep and goats. The rules look a lot like five stones, which children across India play with pebbles.

Gilli-danda uses a long stick and a short one, tapered at both ends. You flick the small one up and whack it as far as you can. Some people think [[@sport-gilli-danda|gilli-danda]] may be an ancestor of cricket and baseball, though the link is debated.

In lagori, also called pittu or seven stones, one team knocks down a pile of flat stones with a ball. Then they must rebuild it while the other team tries to hit them with the ball. Marbles, called kanche in Hindi, have been found in ancient sites from Egypt to the Indus Valley, as told in [[@marbles-tops|marbles and tops]].

{{story:sport-indian-games}}

Before a game starts, kids need to pick who goes first. Around the world, they use counting rhymes. In English, there is "eeny, meeny, miny, moe". Many Indian languages have their own rhymes, sung while pointing round a circle.

Rock-paper-scissors is played almost everywhere. In Japan it is called janken, and versions of it are believed to have come from China centuries ago. In many Indian neighbourhoods, kids also do a quick hand-flip: everyone shows a palm up or down at the same moment, and the odd one out is chosen. Rules vary from street to street, and every group swears its version is the right one.

In the 1950s and 1960s, two British researchers, Iona and Peter Opie, collected games from thousands of children across Britain. They found that children keep games alive for generations, passing them down from older kids to younger ones with little help from adults.

They also found that games change as they travel. A rhyme might lose a line, or a rule might get added in one school and not the next. [[folklore|Folklore]] experts in India and the US have found the same thing.

Kho-kho is a great example of a playground game becoming a sport. It grew from an old chasing game in Maharashtra, got official rules, and is now played in leagues and [[tournament|tournaments]]. In 2025, India hosted the first Kho Kho World Cup.

And the strangest part? Games help children make [[@friendship|friends]] faster than almost anything else, which may be why playgrounds everywhere sound the same, whatever language the shouting is in.

text: Rights are freedoms and protections that every person should have, such as the right to be treated equally, to speak freely, to follow your own religion and to go to school. Duties are responsibilities you have towards others and towards your country, such as obeying the law, respecting other people and protecting the environment.

The two go together. Your right to walk safely down the street depends on other people's duty not to harm you, and theirs depends on yours. In India, rights are written into the [[@constitution|Constitution]] and can be defended in court. Duties are listed there too, but mostly as goals to live by.

myth: Having rights means you can do whatever you want.

Rights have limits, because they must fit with other people's rights. Freedom of speech in India and the USA does not protect, for example, lying about someone in a way that harms them, or calling for violence.

sec.h: Rights you can take to court
sec.t:
Part III of India's Constitution lists the Fundamental Rights. They include the right to equality, the right to [[@free-speech|freedom of speech]] and movement, and protection against forced labour and [[@child-labour|child labour]]. There is freedom of religion, and cultural and educational rights for minorities. Finally, there is the right to go to court to protect all of these.

That last one matters most. If the government breaks your rights, you can go straight to the Supreme Court or a High Court. B. R. [[@ambedkar|Ambedkar]], who led the drafting of the Constitution, called this right its "heart and soul". He knew that rights on paper mean little if nobody can enforce them.

Rights can be added or removed. The right to property was a Fundamental Right until 1978, when it was moved out of that list. In 2002, India added the right to free education for children aged 6 to 14. Courts have also widened the meaning of existing rights. The Supreme Court has said that the right to life includes the right to clean air and water and, since 2017, the right to privacy.

When India's Constitution began in 1950, it had no list of duties. In 1976, the 42nd Amendment added ten Fundamental Duties, and an eleventh was added in 2002. They include respecting the national flag and anthem, protecting forests, rivers and wildlife, developing a scientific temper, and, for parents, giving their children the chance to go to school.

Courts cannot usually punish you just for ignoring a duty. Some critics say that makes them weak. Others say duties work best as shared values, taught at school and at home, rather than as rules backed by fines.

The United States Constitution of 1787 at first said little about individual rights. Many Americans objected, so in 1791 ten [[@constitution-amendments|amendments]] were added, called the Bill of Rights. They protect freedom of speech, religion and the press, and the right to a fair trial. The [[@us-constitution|US Constitution]] has no list of duties like India's, though citizens are expected to obey laws, pay taxes and serve on juries when called.

text: Computers are made of billions of tiny switches that are either on (1) or off (0).
In binary, each switch is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and so on. Add up the "on" switches to get the number. So 1011 means 8 + 0 + 2 + 1, which is 11.

Letters, colours and sounds are all turned into numbers, and the numbers into 1s and 0s. A computer is very good at one thing: flipping huge numbers of switches extremely fast, millions of times in the blink of an eye.

quiz.prompt: In binary, each place is worth double the one to its right (4, 2, 1). What normal number is 101?
quiz.reveal: Read it as switches worth 4, 2 and 1. The 4 is on, the 2 is off and the 1 is on, so 4 + 1 = 5.

myth: Somewhere inside a computer there are tiny written 0s and 1s.
There are no written digits anywhere. 0 and 1 are just names for two states, such as low or high voltage in a chip, or the two ways a speck of a hard disk can be magnetised.

sec.t:
We count in tens, probably because we have [[@maths-binary-fingers|ten fingers]]. A computer has no fingers, only [[@electricity-made|electricity]]. Telling ten different levels of electricity apart would be tricky, because wires pick up small wobbles and noise. Telling two apart is easy: is the current there or not?

That simple choice makes computers reliable. A slightly weak "on" is still clearly on. In 1938, a young American engineer named Claude Shannon showed that [[circuit|circuits]] of on-off switches could do [[@logic|logic]] and arithmetic. His idea is inside every chip made since.

Around 2,000 years ago, the Indian scholar Pingala described poetry [[rhythm|rhythms]] using patterns of [[@maths-music-rhythm|short and long beats]], an early binary-like system. Each line of a poem became a string of two kinds of sounds, like dots and dashes. He even worked out how many patterns of a given length were possible. [[@fibonacci-nature|More from Pingala]].

In 1703, the German mathematician Gottfried Leibniz published a paper on binary counting. He was delighted to learn that patterns in the *I Ching*, an old Chinese book, could be read as binary too.

sec.h: Counting on your fingers, computer style
sec.t:
You can count past ten on your fingers by using binary. Let each finger stand for a place: your thumb is 1, the next finger 2, then 4, 8 and 16. A finger up means on, and a finger down means off.

With one hand, you can show every number from 0 to 31. With both hands, you can reach 1,023. Try showing 7, then 20, then 31. With practice, you can count to over a thousand without taking your shoes off.

sec.h: From numbers to the whole internet
sec.t:
Today, binary connects everything. When you send a photo, your phone breaks it into long strings of 1s and 0s. The [[@internet-how|internet]] carries them as flashes of light in glass cables or as [[@radio-waves|radio waves]], and another device rebuilds the picture.

Even secrets travel in binary. To keep a message private, computers scramble its 1s and 0s using maths, as you can see in [[@cipher-codes|secret codes]]. The switches never know what they are holding. They only know on and off, and that turns out to be enough.

text: Game theory is the maths of decision-making when other people's choices matter too. In a "game", each player picks a strategy, and the result depends on what everyone picks. It could be rock-paper-scissors, a cricket captain choosing whether to bat first, or two shops deciding their prices.

Game theorists ask questions like: what is the smartest choice if the other side is also being smart? When should you cooperate, and when should you compete? These questions turn up in economics, politics, sport, biology and computer science.

st.reveal: If you cut, you know the other person will take the bigger piece, so your best move is to cut as fairly as you can. Neither person can do better by complaining. It is a tiny example of game theory designing a fair rule.

myth: Game theory is only about board games and sports.

The "games" can be any situation where people's choices affect each other. Game theory is used in economics, politics, biology, computer science and even in designing auctions for mobile phone spectrum.

sec.t:
The subject was launched by a book published in 1944, *Theory of Games and Economic Behavior*, by the mathematician John von Neumann and the economist Oskar Morgenstern. They showed that strategy in games such as poker could be studied with careful maths.

In 1950, a young American mathematician named John Nash added a key idea, now called a Nash equilibrium. It is a situation where no player can do better by changing their own choice alone, as long as everyone else sticks to theirs. Nash shared the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1994. His life, including his long struggle with mental illness, was told in the 2001 film *A Beautiful Mind*.

What if the game is played again and again? In 1980, the political scientist Robert Axelrod ran a [[tournament|tournament]] where computer programs played repeated prisoner's dilemmas against each other. The winner was a short program called "tit for tat", sent in by Anatol Rapoport. It cooperated in the first round, then simply copied its opponent's last move.

Tit for tat was nice, because it never cheated first. It hit back when cheated, but forgave as soon as the other player cooperated again. Axelrod argued that strategies like this help explain how cooperation can grow, even among animals.

In some games, being predictable is fatal. In rock-paper-scissors, if you always throw rock, a smart opponent always throws paper. The best plan, mathematically, is to choose each option one-third of the time, at random. Then no opponent can find a pattern.

Football penalties, from school matches to the [[@fifa-world-cup|World Cup]], work in a similar way. A kicker who always shoots to the same side is easy to save. Researchers who studied thousands of professional penalties found that kickers and goalkeepers mix up their choices in ways quite close to what game theory predicts.

During the [[@cold-war|Cold War]], American and Soviet planners used game theory to think about nuclear weapons, where each side's safety depended on what the other believed it might do. Today, game theory helps design auctions and traffic systems. It also guided the [[@ai-what|AI]] programs that, from 2017, began beating top professional poker players, a game full of bluffing and hidden cards.

text: A set is simply a collection of things. The things can be anything: numbers, animals, cities, or the children in your class. The colours of the Indian flag form a set: [[@saffron|saffron]], white, green and navy blue. The even numbers form a set too, an endless one.

A Venn diagram is a picture of sets. Each set is drawn as a circle. Where [[@circles|circles]] overlap, you put the things that belong to both sets. Things outside all the circles belong to none. It is a simple idea, but it helps people sort information, solve puzzles and even design search engines.

st.prompt: In a class of 30, 18 children like mangoes and 15 like chocolate. Every child likes at least one. How many like both?
st.reveal: 18 + 15 = 33, but there are only 30 children. The 3 extra must have been counted twice, once in each circle, so 3 children sit in the overlap and like both.

d.try: Draw two big overlapping circles on paper, or make them on the floor with two loops of string. Label them "has a pet" and "has a sibling". Ask your family or friends and write each name in the right place. Who ends up in the middle, and who stands outside both circles?
myth: Any diagram with overlapping circles is a Venn diagram.

In a true Venn diagram, every possible overlap is drawn, even if some are empty. Diagrams that only show the overlaps that really exist are more properly called Euler diagrams, after the mathematician who used them first.

sec.t:
Mathematicians have special words for combining sets. The union of two sets is everything in either one. The intersection is only what they share. If one set is "children who play cricket" and another is "children who play the flute", the intersection is the children who do both.

There is also the empty set, which has nothing in it at all, like the set of elephants in your pencil box. It sounds silly, but the empty set matters in maths in much the way [[@zero-invent|zero]] matters in counting.

Sets can sit inside other sets too. Every dog is a [[mammal|mammal]], so the set of dogs is a subset of the set of mammals. In a diagram, the dog circle sits completely inside the mammal circle. [[biologist|Biologists]] sort living things this way, in sets within sets, from kingdoms right down to species.

John Venn was an English mathematician and priest who taught at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge. In 1880 he published a paper showing how overlapping circles could make logical arguments easier to see. The diagrams soon took his name.

He was not the first to draw circles this way. More than a century earlier, the Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler had used them in letters teaching logic to a German princess. Venn's idea was to always draw every possible overlap, even the empty ones, so nothing could be missed.

Venn also liked building machines. He made one that bowled cricket balls, and in 1909 it was tested against the touring Australian team. According to his college, it bowled out one of their leading batsmen more than once. Today the college dining hall has a stained-glass window showing a Venn diagram in his memory.

{{story:search-engines}}

When you search online, a [[@search-engines|search engine]] is often working with sets. Search for "tigers India" and it looks for pages in the set containing "tigers" and the set containing "India", then shows you the overlap. Librarians call this AND searching. OR searching gives the union instead, and NOT removes a set.

The same thinking is used in databases, shopping websites and [[@data-science|data science]]. When a website filters shoes by "red" and "size 5", it is finding the intersection of two sets.

In the 1870s, a German mathematician named Georg Cantor began studying sets seriously, including infinite ones. He reached a startling conclusion. Some infinite sets are bigger than others.

The set of counting numbers, 1, 2, 3 and so on, never ends. But Cantor proved that the set of all [[decimal|decimal]] numbers is even bigger, so big that it can never be listed, even with forever to do it. Many mathematicians at the time found this hard to accept. Today, Cantor's set theory is part of the foundations of modern maths, and his ideas about [[@infinity|infinity]] still surprise people meeting them for the first time.

text: Rubber ducks are yellow because they copy baby ducks. Many duck chicks, like those of farm ducks, are covered in fluffy yellow down. Toy makers chose that cheerful colour, and it stuck.

Yellow also helps the toy show up against bathwater and white tiles, which makes it easy for small children to spot and grab. Over the years, the bright yellow duck with an orange beak became one of the most famous toys in the world.
Most rubber ducks today aren't made of rubber at all. They are made of vinyl, a soft plastic that is cheaper and easier to shape.

d.try: Float a rubber duck or a small plastic bottle in a sink or bath, then gently push it under and let go. Notice how hard the water pushes it back up. Now add a few coins inside a bottle and see how much weight it can carry before it sinks.
myth: Rubber ducks are made of rubber.
Early ones were, but most are now made of vinyl, a soft plastic. Toy makers kept the old name because everyone already knew it.

sec.t:
Natural rubber comes from the sap of rubber trees. On its own it goes sticky in heat and hard in cold. In the 1840s, Charles Goodyear found a way to make it stronger and more stable by heating it with sulphur, a process called [[@accident-vulcanised-rubber|vulcanisation]].

After that, factories began making rubber toys, including ducks. Early ones were often solid and didn't float well. In the 1940s, an American sculptor named Peter Ganine designed a duck that could be made in large numbers and floated upright, and he patented it.

Later, makers switched to vinyl. Vinyl ducks are hollow and full of air, which helps them float high on the water. The way air and water hold things up is explained in [[@floating-ships|how ships float]].

In 1970, Ernie, a Muppet on the children's TV show [[@sesame-street|Sesame Street]], sang a song called "Rubber Duckie" to his bath toy. The song became a hit and even reached the American pop charts.

After that, the rubber duck was a star. Ernie's duck became so famous that it later showed up on stamps, lunchboxes and countless bath mats. In 2013, it was added to the National Toy Hall of Fame in the United States, alongside toys like the yo-yo and Lego.

In January 1992, a ship crossing the North Pacific hit a storm. A container fell overboard and broke open. Inside were about 28,800 floating plastic bath toys: yellow ducks, red beavers, blue turtles and green frogs.

The toys drifted for years. Some washed up in Alaska within months. Others travelled much further. Ocean scientist Curtis Ebbesmeyer and his colleagues asked beachcombers to report any they found. The sightings helped them map [[@ocean-currents|ocean currents]], the giant rivers inside the sea.

The sun and salt bleached many of the yellow ducks almost white. Some were reported to have drifted into the Arctic and onwards towards the North Atlantic, though only a few such finds were ever confirmed. People still report the odd faded toy today.

{{story:ocean-plastic}}

In 2007, the Dutch artist Florentijn Hofman made a giant inflatable rubber duck and floated it in a French harbour. Later versions visited cities around the world. In Hong Kong in 2013, a duck about 16.5 metres tall, as high as a five-storey building, drew huge crowds.

Rubber ducks also raise money. In duck races, thousands of numbered ducks are tipped into a river. People pay for a number, and the first duck past the finish line wins a prize.

Computer programmers have their own use. Some keep a duck on their desk and explain their code to it, line by line. It sounds silly, but saying a problem out loud often reveals the mistake. This is called rubber duck debugging, and it's a real trick used in [[@programming|programming]].

And the strangest part? The bath toys lost in 1992 showed scientists how far floating plastic can travel. That lesson matters even more today, as millions of tonnes of plastic rubbish drift through the same currents.

text: The teddy bear is named after Theodore Roosevelt, the 26th president of the United States, whose nickname was Teddy. In November 1902 he went bear hunting in Mississippi. After days with no luck, his guides chased down a black bear and tied it to a tree so the president could shoot it.
Roosevelt refused. He said shooting a tied-up animal would be unsporting. A cartoonist named Clifford Berryman drew the scene for The Washington Post, and the story spread across the country.
A shopkeeper in New York saw the cartoon, sewed a toy bear, and asked to call it "Teddy's bear". The name stuck, and within a few years teddy bears were a craze across America and Europe.

sec.t:
Berryman's drawing was called "Drawing the Line in Mississippi". In it, the president turns away from a small, frightened bear with his hand raised. Newspapers in other cities copied it. Berryman kept drawing the little bear in later cartoons about Roosevelt, and readers grew fond of it.

The hunting guide that week was Holt Collier, a famous hunter who had been born into slavery. He had tracked the bear for the president. His name is often left out of the story, but historians now give him credit.

Roosevelt reportedly never liked the nickname Teddy. He became stuck with it on millions of toys anyway. You can read about other surprises from the White House in [[@usa-presidents-facts|US presidents' oddest facts]].

In Brooklyn, New York, Morris and Rose Michtom ran a small shop selling sweets and stationery. Rose sewed a plush bear and Morris put it in the window beside the cartoon. People wanted to buy it. The bears sold so well that the couple started the Ideal Novelty and Toy Company.

Across the ocean in Germany, the Steiff company had begun as a workshop run by Margarete Steiff, who made felt toys. Her nephew Richard designed a bear with arms and legs that moved. At a toy fair in Leipzig in 1903, an American buyer ordered 3,000 of them.

One of the early Michtom bears now sits in the [[@smithsonian|Smithsonian]] museum in Washington, DC. It has lost much of its fur from being loved. Teddy bears soon became part of Roosevelt's public image, and his supporters used them at rallies and on badges.

{{story:bears-india}}

Once the teddy existed, writers gave bears personalities. Winnie-the-Pooh appeared in 1926. The real Christopher Robin had a teddy, and its name came from Winnipeg, a black bear living at London Zoo. Paddington Bear, from "darkest Peru", arrived in 1958. In India, many children grew up with Jambavan, the wise bear king of the Ramayana, long before teddies reached the shops.

Real bears are nothing like these soft, round friends. Wild bears are strong, fast and best watched from a distance. India has four kinds, from the shaggy sloth bear to the small sun bear, as you can see in [[@bears-india|India's bears]].

Doctors and psychologists call a cuddly toy a comfort object. Many young children carry one through big changes, like starting school or moving house. Police officers and ambulance crews in several countries keep teddy bears in their vehicles to calm frightened children.

Teddies are not just for little kids, either. Plenty of adults keep their childhood bear for life. Some old Steiff bears have sold at auction for huge sums, because collectors love the early designs.

And the strangest part? The cartoon that started it all was made by a political cartoonist, not a toymaker. His craft lives on in [[@famous-cartoonists|the world's best-loved cartoonists]].

text: [[@life-weddings-world|An Indian wedding]] is usually seen as two whole families joining, as well as two people. So aunts, uncles, cousins, neighbours, old school friends and colleagues of both families may all be invited. A guest list of several hundred is common, and some run past a thousand.

There are also many events. A wedding can begin days earlier with henna parties, music nights and prayers, then the wedding itself, then a reception. Each event brings its own clothes, food and guests.
Not every wedding is huge. Plenty of couples choose a small ceremony or a simple court wedding. But the big wedding is a tradition that many families save up for over years.

sec.t:
In much of India, people grow up close to large [[@families-world|families]]. Cousins can feel like brothers and sisters, and an elderly great-aunt expects to be asked. Leaving someone out can cause hurt that lasts for years.

The wedding is also a way of welcoming a new person into a whole network of relatives. Many [[ritual|rituals]] are about the families as much as the couple. In some Hindu weddings the bride's parents give her hand to the groom in a ceremony called kanyadaan. In a Sikh wedding, the Anand Karaj, the couple walks four times around the [[@guru-granth-sahib|Guru Granth Sahib]] while hymns are sung.

Feeding guests well is a matter of pride. A wedding may serve several meals a day, from a breakfast of puris to a dinner of dozens of dishes and a whole table of [[@sweets-india|sweets]]. In parts of South India, the meal is served on [[@south-indian-meals|banana leaves]], with servers walking down long rows of guests.

Big weddings employ many people: cooks, tailors, florists, priests, drummers, photographers, decorators and tent makers. In wedding season, some streets fill with marigold sellers and lights.

Many Hindu families pick a date that astrologers call auspicious, or lucky. These dates come from traditional [[@indian-calendars|Indian calendars]], so thousands of weddings can land on the same few nights. Banquet halls are booked a year ahead, and traffic jams form around wedding venues.

In the USA, a wedding is often a single day, with roughly a hundred guests. Indian American families sometimes blend both styles, with a mehendi on Friday and a church or courthouse wedding on Saturday.

Big weddings are not always happy stories. Some families borrow heavily to pay for them, and feel pushed by what neighbours expect. Dowry, money or gifts demanded from the bride's family, has been illegal in India since 1961, but it still happens in some places. That is why more couples now choose smaller weddings and spend the money on a home or their studies instead.

text: रास्तों में तेज़ होना कुछ हद तक एक हुनर है, जो अभ्यास से बढ़ता है। तुम्हारा दिमाग खास कोशिकाओं की मदद से भीतर एक नक्शा बनाता है। ये कोशिकाएँ हिप्पोकैंपस नाम के हिस्से में होती हैं, जो दिमाग के दोनों तरफ़ भीतर गहराई में है। तुम जितना घूमते-खोजते हो और ध्यान देते हो कि कौन-सी चीज़ कहाँ है, भीतर का यह नक्शा उतना ही पक्का होता जाता है।

कुछ लोग कुदरती तौर पर दूसरों से बेहतर होते हैं, और इसमें [[gene|जीन]] की भी भूमिका हो सकती है। पर तुम कहाँ बड़े हुए, बचपन में कितना पैदल घूमे, और फ़ोन के नक्शों पर कितना टिके रहते हो, ये सब बहुत मायने रखते लगते हैं।

sec.t:
1971 में वैज्ञानिक जॉन ओ’कीफ़ को चूहों के दिमाग में ऐसी कोशिकाएँ मिलीं जो तभी सक्रिय होती थीं जब चूहा किसी एक खास जगह पर होता। उन्होंने इन्हें *प्लेस सेल*, यानी जगह वाली कोशिकाएँ, कहा। बाद में 2005 में नॉर्वे के मे-ब्रिट और एडवर्ड मोज़र ने *ग्रिड सेल* खोजे। जानवर के चलते समय ये त्रिकोणों के एक पैटर्न में सक्रिय होते हैं, जैसे ग्राफ़ पेपर के खाने।

ये कोशिकाएँ मिलकर दिमाग को बताती हैं कि तुम कहाँ हो और किधर जा रहे हो। कुछ और कोशिकाएँ इस हिसाब से सक्रिय होती हैं कि तुम्हारा सिर किस दिशा में है, कुछ-कुछ कंपास की तरह। 2014 में इन खोजों के लिए तीनों वैज्ञानिकों को मिलकर नोबेल पुरस्कार मिला। इंसानों में भी इसी तरह की [[neuron|कोशिकाएँ]] होती हैं।

sec.h: तुम कहाँ बड़े हुए, यह मायने रखता है
sec.t:
2016 में वैज्ञानिकों ने *सी हीरो क्वेस्ट* नाम का एक फ़ोन गेम निकाला, जिसमें खिलाड़ी समुद्री जीव खोजने के लिए नाव चलाते हैं। लगभग 40 लाख लोगों ने इसे खेला। यह रास्ता खोजने पर अब तक के सबसे बड़े अध्ययनों में से एक बन गया।

शोधकर्ताओं ने पाया कि जो लोग गाँव-देहात में, या पुरानी, टेढ़ी-मेढ़ी गलियों वाले शहरों में बड़े हुए, वे औसतन रास्ता खोजने में बेहतर थे। जो लोग सीधे, चौखानेदार शहरों में बड़े हुए, जैसे अमेरिका के बहुत-से शहर, वे थोड़े कमज़ोर निकले। भारत का सबसे जाना-माना चौखानेदार शहर चंडीगढ़ है, जिसे 1950 के दशक में सीधी सड़कों और नंबर वाले सेक्टरों के साथ बसाया गया था। लगता है बचपन में उलझे रास्तों का अभ्यास दिमाग को सधा देता है। पुरानी दिल्ली या बनारस की गलियों में बड़े होने वाले बच्चों के लिए यह अच्छी खबर है।

गेम से देशों के बीच के फ़र्क भी दिखे। पुरुषों ने औसतन महिलाओं से थोड़ा बेहतर किया, पर जिन देशों में पुरुषों और महिलाओं में ज़्यादा बराबरी है, वहाँ यह फ़ासला कम था। इससे लगता है कि इसका बड़ा हिस्सा संस्कृति और अभ्यास से समझा जा सकता है।

sec.h: क्या जीपीएस हमें कमज़ोर बनाता है?
sec.t:
कुछ अध्ययन बताते हैं कि जो लोग हर समय फ़ोन के मोड़-दर-मोड़ निर्देशों के पीछे चलते हैं, उनके भीतर का नक्शा कमज़ोर बनता है। जब तुम बस “200 मीटर बाद बाएँ मुड़ें” मानते जाते हो, तो दिमाग को यह सोचने की ज़रूरत ही नहीं पड़ती कि तुम कहाँ हो।

कुछ संस्कृतियाँ बचपन से ही दिशा का अभ्यास कराती हैं। ऑस्ट्रेलिया में गुगु यिमिधिर बोलने वाले हमेशा दिशाओं के नाम इस्तेमाल करते हैं, इसलिए उन्हें हमेशा पता रहता है कि उत्तर किधर है। प्रशांत महासागर के द्वीपों के लोग कभी तारों, लहरों और पक्षियों को पढ़कर हज़ारों किलोमीटर समुद्र पार कर जाते थे।

जानवरों की अपनी तरकीबें हैं। संदेशवाहक [[@pigeons-homing|कबूतर]] सैकड़ों किलोमीटर दूर से लौट आते हैं, शायद सूरज, गंध और धरती के [[@earth-magnet|चुंबकीय क्षेत्र]] की मदद से। उधर तुम्हारा फ़ोन बहुत ऊपर घूमते [[orbit|उपग्रहों]] से आते संकेतों का समय नापकर तुम्हें ढूँढता है, जैसा [[@gps-how|जीपीएस कैसे काम करता है]] में समझाया गया है। किसी बड़े के साथ छोटी, सुरक्षित सैर पर इसे बंद कर दो, और कसरत तुम्हारे हिप्पोकैंपस की हो जाएगी।

text: 2016 के एक सावधान अनुमान के मुताबिक तुम्हारा शरीर लगभग 38 लाख करोड़ बैक्टीरिया का घर है। यह मोटे तौर पर तुम्हारी अपनी सारी कोशिकाओं जितना है, जो लगभग 30 लाख करोड़ हैं। गिनती इतनी बड़ी है कि अगर तुम हर सेकंड एक बैक्टीरिया गिनो, तो तुम्हें दस लाख साल से भी ज़्यादा लगेंगे।

इनमें से लगभग सभी बेकसूर हैं, और बहुत-से काम के हैं। ये खाना पचाने में मदद करते हैं, विटामिन बनाते हैं, तुम्हारे [[immune-system|प्रतिरक्षा तंत्र]] को सिखाते हैं और नुकसानदेह कीटाणुओं को जगह नहीं लेने देते। तुम्हारे साथ रहने वाले सारे [[microbe|सूक्ष्मजीवों]] को मिलाकर माइक्रोबायोम कहते हैं। तुम्हारे सारे बैक्टीरिया मिलाकर बस लगभग 0.2 किलो के होते हैं, करीब एक छोटे आम जितने।

text: The Silk Road was a huge network of trade routes that linked [[@china-today|China]] with Central Asia, India, Persia, Arabia and the Mediterranean. It was busiest from about the 2nd century BCE to the 15th century CE.

Merchants carried Chinese silk west, and brought back horses, glass, gold and wool. Indian [[@spices|spices]], cotton and gems joined the flow. Along with goods came ideas. Buddhism travelled from India to China, paper-making moved west from China, and numbers, foods, music and diseases spread too. Most traders covered only one stretch, then sold their goods on, so the Silk Road worked like a giant relay rather than a single journey.

sec.t:
The Chinese learned to make silk thousands of years ago, from the [[cocoon|cocoons]] of silkworms that feed on mulberry leaves. For centuries they kept the method secret. Rich Romans paid high prices for this smooth, light cloth and had no idea how it was made.

The Byzantine historian Procopius wrote that, around the 550s CE, monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Constantinople, the capital of the eastern Roman Empire, perhaps hidden in hollow walking sticks. After that, Europe began making its own [[@silk|silk]].

Buddhist monks used the same routes as traders. Statues, cave temples and texts appeared along the way, mixing Indian, Greek and Chinese styles.

The Chinese monk Xuanzang walked to India in the 7th century to study at [[@nalanda|Nalanda]], and returned with hundreds of texts. Near Dunhuang, the Mogao Caves hold hundreds of painted Buddhist shrines. In one sealed cave, a copy of the Diamond Sutra was found, printed in 868 CE. It is the oldest dated printed book known, and it is now in the British Library in London.

Goods also moved by sea, from Chinese ports past Southeast Asia to India, Arabia and East Africa. Sailors used the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] winds, which blow one way in summer and the other way in winter.

Indian ports on the Malabar and Coromandel coasts were busy stops. [[@cardamom-pepper|Pepper]] from [[@kerala|Kerala]] was so prized in Rome that Roman coins have been dug up in south India. Hoards of them have turned up in Tamil Nadu and Kerala, some still in the pots their owners buried.

At Arikamedu, near [[@puducherry|Puducherry]], [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] found pieces of Roman wine jars and fine Roman pottery. Ships sailing with the summer [[monsoon|monsoon]] could cross from the Red Sea to India in a few weeks, and return with the winter winds.

From the 15th century, European ships found sea routes around Africa to India and China. Land routes became less important, and [[empire|empires]] along them rose and fell.

Today, the old routes have a new fame. In 2014 UNESCO listed a 5,000 km section running from China into Central Asia as a [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage Site]]. Silk still comes from China and India, but now it travels in shipping containers.

text: Dubai grew from a small trading town into a giant modern city in just a few decades. It began with a natural harbour, the Dubai Creek, and a ruling family that welcomed traders. Oil, found in 1966, paid for roads, ports and airports. But Dubai's oil was never huge, so its rulers used the money to turn the city into a hub for trade, flights, banking and tourism.
In 2025 Dubai passed 4 million people. Around nine in ten of them come from other countries, and the largest group is from India.

sec.t:
In 1833, members of the Bani Yas tribe, led by the Al Maktoum family, settled by the creek. The Al Maktoums still rule Dubai today. Fishing and [[@pearls|pearl diving]] were the main work. Divers held their breath for a minute or more as they dropped to the sea floor to collect oysters, coming up again and again through long hot days.

The pearl trade collapsed in the 1930s, when Japan began farming cheaper cultured pearls. Dubai then made its money from trade, with dhows, wooden sailing boats, carrying goods to and from India, Iran and East Africa. Old houses in the Al Fahidi area still have wind towers, tall chimneys that catch breezes and send them down into the rooms to cool them.

For many years, Dubai and its neighbours used Indian money. From 1959 to 1966, the Reserve Bank of India even printed a special Gulf rupee for use in the region. Ties with India are still strong. Indian schools, temples and restaurants are found across the city, and flights connect Dubai to dozens of Indian cities.

In 1966, [[@oil-coal|oil]] was found off Dubai's coast, and [[export|exports]] began in 1969. In 1971, Dubai joined six other emirates to form the United Arab Emirates. Its rulers knew the oil would not last forever. They dredged the creek, built Jebel Ali port, one of the largest human-made harbours in the world, and set up zones where foreign companies could do business easily.

Today oil makes up only a tiny share of Dubai's [[economy|economy]]. Dubai International Airport is [[@extreme-busiest-places|one of the world's busiest]] for international passengers.

Dubai's skyline rose fast. The Burj Khalifa, opened in 2010, is about 828 m tall, more than twice the height of the Empire State Building. Its Y-shaped base and stepped shape help it stand up to desert winds, and its [[@elevators|elevators]] are some of the fastest in the world. On a clear day you can see the top from about 95 km away.

{{story:deserts-sand}}

Dubai also built islands. Palm Jumeirah, shaped like a palm tree, was made by spraying millions of cubic metres of [[@sand-where|sand]] dredged from the sea floor. You might wonder why they didn't use [[@deserts-sand|desert sand]]. Its grains have been rolled by wind until they are too smooth and round to pack firmly or make good concrete.

Summer temperatures in Dubai often pass 40 °C, and sometimes 45 °C. Almost everything is [[@air-conditioning|air-conditioned]], from malls to bus stops. Rain is rare, so drinking water comes from desalination plants that remove salt from seawater. These use lots of energy, and the city is building large [[@future-energy|solar farms]] in the desert. Out in the dunes, people still race [[@camels|camels]], now often guided by small robot jockeys.

text: Egypt gets almost no rain. Without the Nile, it would be almost entirely desert. The river brings water for drinking and farming, a road for boats, and in the past, rich black mud spread by its yearly [[@floods-why|floods]]. The ancient Greek historian Herodotus called Egypt "the gift of the Nile".

Today Egypt has more than 10 crore people, and about 95% of them live within a short distance of the river or its delta. All that life is squeezed onto about 5% of the country's land. From space, the Nile looks like a green line drawn across a sandy page.

sec.t:
The Nile has two main branches. The White Nile flows from the region of Lake Victoria in East Africa. The Blue Nile starts at Lake Tana in the highlands of [[@ethiopia|Ethiopia]]. They meet at Khartoum in Sudan and flow north together through the desert to Egypt and the Mediterranean Sea.

Every summer, [[monsoon|monsoon]] rains fall on the Ethiopian highlands. The Blue Nile swells and carries huge loads of mud downstream. That is what used to cause Egypt's yearly flood.

For thousands of years, the Nile flooded Egypt every summer, from about June to September. When the water went down, it left a layer of dark, [[fertile|fertile]] mud. Farmers planted wheat and barley in it. The ancient Egyptians called their country Kemet, "the black land", after this soil. The desert around it was Deshret, "the red land".

The flood was so important that the Egyptians measured it carefully with nilometers, stone steps or columns marked with levels. A good flood meant a good harvest, and taxes were set to match. Too little water meant hunger. Too much washed away villages.

sec.h: A river that shaped a civilisation

sec.t:
In 1970, Egypt finished the Aswan High Dam. It holds back Lake Nasser, one of the largest human-made lakes in the world. The dam ended the yearly floods, provided water all year round and makes a large amount of [[@dams-power|electricity]].

There were costs. The rising lake would have drowned ancient temples. In the 1960s, UNESCO led a worldwide effort to save them. The great temples of Abu Simbel were cut into more than 1,000 huge blocks and rebuilt about 65 m higher. Without the flood's mud, farmers now need [[fertiliser|fertilisers]], and the [[@deltas|delta]] on the coast is slowly shrinking.

The Nile passes through or drains parts of 11 countries. In 2011, Ethiopia began building a large dam on the Blue Nile, the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, to make electricity for its people, and officially opened it in 2025. Egypt and Sudan worry that it could reduce the water reaching them. The three countries have held many talks, and they still disagree on how the river should be shared.

text: Puerto Rico is a [[tropical|tropical]] island in the Caribbean Sea, about 1,600 kilometres south-east of [[@miami|Miami]]. It has belonged to the United States since 1898, but it is not a state. It is a [[territory|territory]], a place governed by the USA without the full powers of a state.

Puerto Ricans have been US citizens since 1917. They can live and work anywhere in the country. But while they live on the island, they cannot vote for the president, and they send only one member to Congress, who cannot vote on final laws. About 33 lakh people live on the island, and even more people of Puerto Rican heritage live in the mainland USA. Most islanders speak [[@spanish-language|Spanish]] at home, and many speak English too.

sec.t:
The first people to live here were the Taíno, who called the island Borikén. [[@columbus|Columbus]] arrived in 1493 on his second voyage, and Spain ruled for the next four centuries. Many Taíno died from war, forced labour and new diseases, and Spain later brought enslaved Africans to work on sugar farms. Puerto Rican culture today mixes Taíno, Spanish and African roots, from its food to its music.

To guard the harbour of San Juan, Spain built a massive stone fort, El Morro, starting in 1539. Its walls are several metres thick. In 1898, after the Spanish–American War, Spain handed Puerto Rico to the USA.

The island punches above its size in music and sport. Salsa and reggaeton grew partly here, and the 2017 hit song "Despacito" was by two Puerto Rican singers. The [[@baseball-world-series|baseball]] star Roberto Clemente, from the town of Carolina, died in a plane crash in 1972 while carrying relief supplies to earthquake survivors in Nicaragua.

Puerto Ricans disagree about the island's future. Some want it to become the 51st [[@states-usa|US state]]. Some want to keep the current arrangement, and a smaller number want full independence. The island has held several votes on the question since the 1960s, with different results and different levels of turnout. Any change would also need the US Congress to agree, so the debate continues.

{{story:bioluminescence}}

El Yunque, in the north-east, is the only tropical rainforest in the US national forest system. Its mountains catch clouds blowing in from the Atlantic, and some peaks receive several metres of rain a year. It is home to the coquí, a frog only about as long as your thumb, whose loud night-time call gave it its name.

Puerto Rico also has some of the brightest [[@bioluminescence|bioluminescent]] bays in the world. In Mosquito Bay on Vieques, tiny single-celled creatures called dinoflagellates flash when the water moves. Fish leave glowing trails, and a hand trailed in the water looks as if it is covered in stars.

The island sits in the path of Atlantic [[@hurricanes|hurricanes]]. In September 2017, Hurricane Maria struck directly. It knocked out electricity across the whole island, and some homes waited months to get it back. Thousands of people died in the months that followed, many because hospitals and medical equipment lost power.

For over fifty years, Puerto Rico was also home to the Arecibo Observatory, a radio [[@telescopes-how|telescope]] with a dish 305 metres wide set into a bowl in the hills. It studied planets, [[asteroid|asteroids]] and distant [[galaxy|galaxies]], and appeared in films. In 2020, after cables snapped, the platform above it crashed into the dish, and the telescope was not rebuilt.

text: The Panchatantra uses animals because animals make lessons easier to swallow. A story about a foolish lion or a sly jackal can teach a hard truth about power, trust and greed without insulting any real person. Readers recognise human types in the animals, laugh at them and remember the lesson.

The book's own opening tells why it was written. A king named Amarashakti despaired of his three dull sons, who hated their lessons. A wise old scholar named Vishnu Sharma promised to teach them the art of wise living, called *niti*, in six months. He did it with stories, and the princes learned.

sec.t:
*Pancha* means five and *tantra* can mean a treatise or book, so Panchatantra means "five books". Each book has a main story with many smaller [[fable|fables]] tucked inside, as characters tell each other tales to prove a point. The five books deal with losing friends, winning friends, war and peace, losing what you have gained, and acting without thinking.

The first book follows two jackals, Karataka and Damanaka, at a lion's court. The scheming Damanaka breaks up the lion's friendship with a bull, with sad results. It's a lesson for a ruler about trusting flattering advisers.

In "The Lion and the Hare", a greedy lion demands one animal a day for his dinner. When it's the hare's turn, he arrives late and tells the lion that another lion stopped him. He leads the angry lion to a well, where it sees its own reflection, leaps in to attack its "rival", and never climbs out.

In "The Monkey and the Crocodile", a crocodile invites his [[@monkeys-langur|monkey]] friend home on his back, then admits halfway across the river that his wife wants to eat the monkey's heart. Thinking fast, the monkey says he left his heart up in the fruit tree and must fetch it. Once safely back in the branches, he stays there. In "The Tortoise and the Geese", a tortoise carried through the sky on a stick opens its mouth to chatter, and falls.

sec.h: A book that travelled the world
sec.t:
In the 500s CE, a Persian doctor named Burzoe is said to have carried the Panchatantra from India to the court of King Khosrow I and translated it into Middle Persian. In the 700s, the writer Ibn al-Muqaffa turned it into Arabic as *Kalila wa Dimna*, named after the two jackals. From Arabic it passed into Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Spanish and German.

In the 1600s, the French poet Jean de La Fontaine said some of his famous fables were inspired by the Indian sage "Pilpay". The name probably comes from Bidpai, the storyteller of the Arabic version. Today the stories reach children through books, cartoons, [[@amar-chitra-katha|Amar Chitra Katha]] comics and hundreds of [[@translation|translations]].

text: Children's books in India are written by poets, teachers, journalists, scientists and even an engineer who became one of the country's best-loved storytellers. Some, like Ruskin Bond and Sudha Murty, are household names. Many more write in Bengali, Marathi, Tamil, Malayalam, Hindi and other languages for readers in their own corner of the country.

Behind them are publishers big and small, illustrators, translators and libraries. Together they have built a world of Indian stories, so that a child in Kochi or Kanpur can read about places that look like home.

sec.t:
One of the earliest stars was Sukumar Ray. His Bengali book of [[@sukumar-ray|nonsense verse]], *Abol Tabol*, came out in 1923 and is still recited by children in Kolkata. His son, the film-maker Satyajit Ray, later wrote the Feluda detective stories and edited *Sandesh*, the children's magazine his grandfather Upendrakishore Ray Chowdhury had started in 1913. Three generations of one family kept Bengali children reading for most of a century.

Ruskin Bond, born in 1934, has written for more than seventy years. His stories about the hills around Mussoorie and Dehradun, such as *The Blue Umbrella*, read like letters from a friend. He still lives in Landour, near Mussoorie, and children write to him from all over India. In Gujarat, a teacher named Gijubhai Badheka wrote simple stories for small children in the 1920s and changed how many schools thought about early learning.

From the 1990s, new publishers changed what Indian picture books looked like. Tulika Books in Chennai and Tara Books, also in Chennai, worked with folk artists and printed stories in several languages at once. Pratham Books, started in 2004, set out to put "a book in every child's hand" at a low price.

Writers today cover everything from cricket to [[climate|climate]]. Paro Anand writes about hard subjects for teenagers. Ranjit Lal writes about birds and animals, often with plenty of jokes. Subhadra Sen Gupta, who died in 2021, made Indian history lively for young readers. And Sudha Murty's grandmother tales sell in huge numbers in both English and Kannada.

India has 22 languages listed in its Constitution and hundreds of others, which makes [[@translation|translation]] a big part of children's publishing. A good story written in Marathi may reach far more children once it is translated into Hindi or English.

Pratham Books' free website, StoryWeaver, launched in 2015. Anyone can read, print or translate its picture books, and volunteers have produced versions in hundreds of [[@languages-india|languages]]. A child in a village where nobody has ever printed a book in her mother tongue can now read one on a school tablet.

The Sahitya Akademi, India's national academy of letters, gives the Bal Sahitya Puraskar to children's writers in 24 languages each year. Book fairs in Kolkata, Delhi and other cities draw huge crowds of families. The Kolkata fair, held every winter, is one of the busiest book fairs anywhere, and many children buy their first book of their own there. Smaller fairs and school libraries matter just as much. A writer can only reach a child if the book is actually on a shelf nearby.

लगभग हर संस्कृति कोई न कोई अनाज उगाती है और आग जलाना जानती है, इसलिए लगभग हर संस्कृति ने पैनकेक ईजाद किया। फ़र्क़ बस अनाज और बनाने के तरीक़े का है। भारत चावल, [[@lentils-world|दालों]] और बेसन से [[@dosa-idli|डोसा]], उत्तपम और चीला बनाता है। इथियोपिया टेफ़ इस्तेमाल करता है। फ़्रांस गेहूँ से पतले क्रेप बनाता है, और अमेरिकी लोग बेकिंग पाउडर डालकर मोटे, फूले-फूले पैनकेकों का ढेर लगाते हैं। चीन में जियानबिंग है, रूस में ब्लिनी, और [[@seoul|कोरिया]] में पाजॉन, जो हरे प्याज़ से भरा पैनकेक है।
